intro: This unit slows down. Earlier units walked through the whole Bible; this one stays inside the four gospels and reads a few chapters closely. First comes the teaching of Jesus: the long sermon in Matthew 5–7, its shorter cousin in Luke 6, and the parables, short stories that end with a turn. Then come the last chapters of each gospel, the Passion narratives, which describe one Friday four times, and the accounts of an empty tomb.

Close reading means noticing. Which gospel says "the poor" and which says "the poor in spirit"? Which manuscripts end Mark at 16:8? What does Luke's Jesus say from the cross that John's does not? Every difference is evidence of what a writer chose, and every reader, Jewish, Christian, Muslim, secular, brings a way of reading. This unit teaches you to name the text, the writer, the manuscript and the reader before you say what a passage means.

By the end you will be able to compare parallel gospel passages, explain how a parable works, describe what historians can and cannot say about Jesus of Nazareth, and state how Jewish, Christian and Muslim traditions each understand him, without deciding for anyone which is right. That is the skill a public school can teach, and it is a skill you can use on any text.
bigQuestion: How can a reader study the sayings, stories and death of Jesus closely, as history and literature, while respecting the many ways they are believed?

test.q: The Sermon on the Mount is found in which chapters?
test.why: Matthew 5–7 is the Sermon on the Mount. Luke 6 holds the shorter Sermon on the Plain.

test.q: Which blessing appears in Luke without Matthew's qualifier "in spirit"?
choices: Blessed are the pure in heart
test.why: Luke 6:20 says "blessed be ye poor"; Matthew 5:3 says "poor in spirit." The other three are only in Matthew.

test.q: "An eye for an eye" in the antitheses is a quotation from which book?
test.why: Exodus 21:24 states the law of equal retaliation, which Matthew 5:38 quotes.

test.q: Why is the doxology of the Lord's Prayer printed in the King James Version but footnoted in most modern translations?
choices: Modern translators think it is too long
The oldest manuscripts of Matthew lack it
test.why: The doxology is missing from the oldest manuscripts, so scholars judge it a later addition from church practice.

test.q: In the parable of the Good Samaritan, who are the two who pass by?
choices: A tax collector and a soldier
test.why: Luke 10:31–32 names a priest and a Levite. The Samaritan is the one who stops.

test.q: What makes the parable of the laborers in the vineyard uncomfortable?
choices: All workers receive the same pay for unequal hours
test.why: Everyone gets the agreed denarius, so no one is cheated, yet equal pay for unequal work feels unfair. That discomfort is the parable's point.

test.q: Hillel's saying "what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor" is found where?
test.why: The Talmud records Hillel's answer to the man who asked to learn the Torah on one foot. Tobit has a similar rule but not Hillel's words.

test.q: What does the term Synoptic Gospels mean?
choices: The gospels in the Catholic Bible only
Matthew, Mark and Luke, which can be seen together in parallel
The four gospels combined into one
test.why: Synoptic means seen together; Matthew, Mark and Luke share enough material to be laid in columns. John stands apart.

test.q: Which gospel shows Jesus stepping forward to meet his arresters with no anguished prayer?
test.why: John 18 has no Gethsemane prayer; Jesus asks whom they seek and the soldiers fall back.

choices: Blaming Jews as a people for the death of Jesus
Study of the Bible in public schools
test.why: The Vatican declaration stated the Passion cannot be charged against all Jews then or now.

test.q: Which gospels record "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
test.why: Mark 15:34 and Matthew 27:46 record the cry from Psalm 22. Luke and John give other sayings.

test.q: Where do Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus end the Gospel of Mark?
test.why: Both fourth-century manuscripts end at 16:8, with the women afraid and silent.

test.q: What does Tacitus, Annals 15.44, say about Christus?
choices: He taught the Sermon on the Mount
He was executed by Pontius Pilate under Tiberius
test.why: Tacitus records only the execution under Pilate in Tiberius's reign, in his account of Nero and the fire of Rome.

test.q: How does Jewish tradition understand Jesus?
choices: As the messiah who has already come
As a Jewish teacher of the Second Temple period, not the messiah and not divine
As a prophet who was not crucified
test.why: Judaism awaits a human messiah who brings visible peace and holds that God is not a human being. The last choice describes the Muslim view.

test.q: What did Abington v. Schempp (1963) permit in public schools?
choices: Objective study of the Bible's literary and historic qualities
test.why: The Court ended devotional exercises but said objective study as part of a secular education is consistent with the Constitution.

write.prompt: Pick one scene the gospels tell more than once: a beatitude (Matthew 5:3 and Luke 6:20), the garden (Mark 14:32–42 and John 18:1–11), or the empty tomb (Mark 16:1–8 and John 20:1–18). Quote or closely paraphrase both, list every difference, and explain what each writer's choices show about his portrait of Jesus. Then say how a Christian reader and a historian would each use those differences.
tips: Name each passage by gospel, chapter and verse, and say which translation you used.
Attribute every belief: Christians believe, most scholars think, Jewish tradition holds, Muslims read.
Compare the two texts; do not decide which is right.
Use the unit's terms: Synoptic, redaction, criterion, parable, Passion.
End with what a careful reader can say and what the text leaves open.
